messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: contributor copyright agreement?
parts:
Now that we're taking contributions from the outside world,
I'd like to rethink our approach to intellectual property.

The basic geography of IP in the United States is:

* Copyright protects original works of authorship
(for example, the Stan C++ or RStan R/C++ code or the Stan doc)

* a patent protects inventions or discoveries
(for example, the NUTS algorithm)

* a trademark protects words, phrases, symbols, or designs
(for example, the name "Stan" or the Stan logo)

You can think of the copyright, patent, or trademark holder
as the "owner" of a piece of intellectual property.

By default, everything a person writes is automatically
copyrighted to the author upon creation.

A copyright owner may transfer copyright to another legal entity,
such as another person or a company such as a university or a publisher.

Licensing is a separate issue. The owner of a copyrighted work
may license the copyrighted work to another legal entity under
a fixed set of terms layed out in the license.

Our current operating procedure for copyright followed the
Eigen matrix lib approach, so that

1. Stan, RStan and the Stan documentation is copyright to the development
team jointly.

Our procedures for licensing are that

2. Stan C++ code is licensed under the open-source new BSD license,

3. RStan C++ and R code is licensed under the GPLv3 license, and

4. Stan doc is licensed under the most liberal Creative Commons license.

I think we all agree that we should keep the licensing as is. But
what about copyright?

OPTION A. Maintain the current approach to copyright, which requires
all contributors to reassign the copyright for their contribution
to the development team.

OPTION B. Let everyone keep the copyright for whatever they write,
but require that they license it under 2--4 depending on whether
it is for Stan, RStan or for doc.

For example, the Coin-OR foundation (http://www.coin-or.org) for
operations research software uses a license following option B:

http://www.coin-or.org/Ots/license.html

Eigen, the matrix lib we use, follows option A.

Both options require that the developer of the code actually own the
copyright to what they wrote. This is often not the case due to
employment agreements that broadly assign copyright for all code
created to the employer.

- Bob (who is not a lawyer and already has a headache from all this)

P.S. This FAQ is useful on US copyright law (I cribbed the bullet points
above from it):

http://www.copyright.gov/help/faq/faq-general.html

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] contributor copyright agreement?
parts:
My understanding is that option A is actually almost impossible to do
without having people sign things and mail them before their code can
be included. Or, at least, every open source project which requires
copyright assignment that I know of requires this. It's extremely
tedious and a drag on new contributors.

The primary reason to centralize copyright is to make it easier to
relicense things at a later date. The other big reason is to make
enforcement of the license easier. Given that the BSD license is
about as liberal as it gets, both of these seem unlikely, so I would
suggest option B.

Finally, I think the only reasonable thing we can do is assume that
contributors own the code they submit. Obviously, if someone doesn't
and we find out it will need to be removed, but otherwise I'm not sure
what we can do on that front.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] contributor copyright agreement?
parts:
On 5/14/13 5:20 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> My understanding is that option A is actually almost impossible to do
> without having people sign things and mail them before their code can
> be included. Or, at least, every open source project which requires
> copyright assignment that I know of requires this. It's extremely
> tedious and a drag on new contributors.
>
> The primary reason to centralize copyright is to make it easier to
> relicense things at a later date. The other big reason is to make
> enforcement of the license easier. Given that the BSD license is
> about as liberal as it gets, both of these seem unlikely, so I would
> suggest option B.

I came to the same conclusion, hence the message.

I think option A also simplifies things from a business who wants to
use the code point of view. With option B (everyone owns their
contributions, but the product is a big mishmash of all of this), it's
a little scary for a business who wants to use the code.
But then I'm not too worried about that --- if they want to use our
code for free, let them assume that risk.

> Finally, I think the only reasonable thing we can do is assume that
> contributors own the code they submit. Obviously, if someone doesn't
> and we find out it will need to be removed, but otherwise I'm not sure
> what we can do on that front.

Have them get institutional approval from someone at
their employer or to sign something saying they own it.

I haven't interacted with a non-author copyright journal or
proceedings in almost 15 years (everyhting in natural language went
open source ages ago), so I can't recall how publishers
deal with the same issue. Or journals who publish code.

- Bob

But how do we know who needs to do that or not? We can look at email

now) in which you certify that you have the rights to the content.
But they require that of everyone.

Cheers,
